ORIGINAL USMLE-STYLE PRACTICE

When drainage is needed

A 19-year-old has severe unilateral odynophagia and a 2.5-cm peritonsillar collection confirmed on ultrasound. He is protecting his airway but cannot drink because of pain. After analgesia and IV fluids, which treatment strategy is most appropriate?

  1. ENT drainage assessment plus antibiotics
  2. Oral antibiotics alone with outpatient review in a week
  3. A single corticosteroid dose followed by discharge
  4. Immediate tonsillectomy without considering other drainage approaches
  5. Repeat imaging after 72 hours without starting treatment
Answer and explanation

ENT drainage assessment plus antibiotics

A sizable symptomatic abscess requires source-control assessment and antimicrobial therapy; hydration supports recovery.

Option explanations

ENT drainage assessment plus antibiotics: A sizable symptomatic abscess requires source-control assessment and antimicrobial therapy; hydration supports recovery.

Oral antibiotics alone with outpatient review in a week: A sizable confirmed collection and inability to drink warrant drainage assessment and supervised care.

A single corticosteroid dose followed by discharge: Steroids may relieve symptoms as an adjunct but do not replace antimicrobial therapy and source-control assessment.

Immediate tonsillectomy without considering other drainage approaches: Tonsillectomy is appropriate in selected situations, but is not mandatory for every first presentation.

Repeat imaging after 72 hours without starting treatment: A confirmed symptomatic abscess already needs treatment; delaying solely for repeat imaging is inappropriate.
